strengths: Novel application of cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) for discovering computational circuits in protein language models with explicit inter-layer dependency modeling, addressing a meaningful gap between SAE-based interpretability and mechanistic circuit tracing

Strong empirical validation with comprehensive baselines (PLT, SAE, CAA, random), proper train/validation/test protocols, and consistent performance recovery (82-89% on protein family classification) across multiple independent tasks

Compelling biological validation showing discovered circuits align with known structural features (kinase domain HRD motif, NADP+ binding sites, GB1 protein interaction residues) demonstrating practical interpretability value
Complete end-to-end framework combining discovery, steering, and visualization components with well-engineered interactive tools and promised code release enabling reproducibility
Thorough experimental design with detailed appendices covering ablations, implementation details, and comprehensive steering experiments with multiple intervention strategies
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope (single 6-layer ESM2 model) with no validation on deeper architectures; scalability of O(L²) CLT training with model depth unaddressed, raising questions about applicability to modern large-scale protein models

Core assumption that layer ℓ output decomposes into functions of sparse preceding-layer latents remains empirically unvalidated; significant performance degradation in sequential/full replacement models (Figure 5) suggests assumption violations

Moderate technical novelty—circuit discovery algorithms largely adapted from Natsumura et al. (2025) with main contribution being application of CLTs; relationship to SAE-based methods not sufficiently differentiated

Steering and protein engineering claims (79% fitness improvement, high-fitness variant generation) lack rigorous quantitative validation—only visual sequence inspection shown without independent fitness assays or structural predictions

Statistical rigor gaps including large error bars (±0.21 in Table 1), absence of significance testing, and unclear sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., K=1% sparsity chosen without justification or ablation studies)

strengths: Technically sound methodology: CLT formulation is mathematically clear with reasonable training objectives combining reconstruction and sparsity losses

Comprehensive experimental framework: Multiple downstream tasks (protein family classification, function prediction, steering), rigorous circuit definitions based on F1 scores, systematic gradient-based discovery algorithm
Well-designed visualization tools: The interactive interface for exploring circuits, latent rankings, sequence alignments, and influence graphs is well-thought-out and documented
Extensive supplementary material: 26 pages of appendices with implementation details, architectural specifications, hyperparameters, and additional experimental results
Multiple replacement model variants: Direct, sequential, and full replacement models with honest discussion of tradeoffs and reconstruction error propagation
weaknesses: Causality not established: While circuits are defined as latent variables 'responsible for specified behavior,' validation relies on F1 score recovery of latents, not causal inference. Steering experiments only cover 7 DMS assays—insufficient for validating the broad set of discovered circuits

Core assumption unvalidated: Claims that CLTs 'faithfully emulate' internal computation assume sparse cross-layer latents capture essential computation, but reconstruction error and information loss are not systematically analyzed

Weak and missing baselines: PLT baseline is information-starved by design (no cross-layer signals). SAE comparisons are theoretical rather than empirical. No comparison to existing mechanistic interpretability circuit discovery methods makes it impossible to assess relative merit

Unconvincing practical improvements: Steering results show marginal, overlapping-error-bar improvements (Figure 8: ProtoMech 0.40±0.18 vs ESM2 0.39±0.04 when F1<0.5; Figure 5b: ProtoMech vs PLT both 0.38±0.18). These don't support claims about circuit utility for practical applications

Biological discoveries are rediscoveries: Identified circuits (kinase domains, NADP+ binding sites, G-protein mutations) validate known biology from InterPro and literature rather than discovering novel insights. No experimental validation that identified latents causally drive biological function

Unjustified design choices with no ablation: Critical hyperparameters (6 latents per layer, ~1.8% sparsity enforced via TopK, F1=0.7 circuit threshold, max 1000 latents) lack justification and sensitivity analysis

Critical scalability limitations: Acknowledged O(L²) parameter scaling (page 8) prevents application to modern large models. Only ESM2 (6 layers) tested; generalization to larger architectures with >50 layers is entirely unclear

Narrow scope and limited validation: Only one model studied. Steering only on 7 DMS assays from Table 2. No demonstration of enabling new protein design capabilities or discovering functional improvements beyond marginal error-bar overlaps

Overclaimed conclusions: Abstract and main text claim to 'faithfully reproduce' computation and 'discover circuits' without sufficient empirical evidence. The framework validates known biology rather than discovering novel computational principles

Incomplete comparison to related work: SAE-based interpretability approaches dismissed as unsuitable without empirical comparison. No engagement with prior work on mechanistic interpretability in language models beyond brief literature review

strengths: Technically sound methodology: Cross-layer transcoders extend standard transcoders with explicit inter-layer computation (Eq. 1-2), well-motivated for capturing transformer circuit behavior

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple independent evaluations (protein family classification F1=0.82±0.19, function prediction Spearman=0.41±0.19) across 12 DMS assays with proper data splits and uncertainty quantification

Strong biological grounding: Discovered circuits correspond to known functional domains (protein kinase HRD motif, NADP+ binding, GB1 interaction surfaces) with detailed structural validation and mutation sensitivity analysis
Excellent reproducibility: Extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, training procedures in appendices; transparent evaluation metrics; promise of code and tool availability

Useful practical contributions: Interactive visualization tool with multiple views (Figs. 9-14) enables exploration of latent activations, alignments, and circuit dependencies; steerable sequences demonstrate steering capability
Rigorous ablation studies: Systematic comparison of replacement models (direct, sequential, full) isolates CLT contributions; validates architectural choices
Clear presentation: Well-organized narrative with effective figures explaining concepts; consistent mathematical notation; thorough appendices support main claims
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: CLTs extend Amresen et al. (2025) transcoders by summing over prior layers (straightforward modification); circuit discovery adapts existing techniques from language model interpretability rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts
Limited discovery of novel circuits: Most validated circuits correspond to known biological motifs; few unexpected findings that advance biological understanding beyond structural knowledge
Domain-specific scope limits impact: Contribution primarily relevant to protein LM community; limited relevance to broader ICML machine learning audience despite solid work
Incomplete comparisons: Appendix G briefly argues CLTs outperform SAEs but lacks empirical evaluation on common tasks; comparison remains largely conceptual rather than quantitative
Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: CLT training balance (α_aux) and TopK sparsity threshold not thoroughly analyzed; robustness to these choices unclear
Code and tool availability not clearly specified: Paper states 'code can be found at' and mentions visualizer availability but specific URLs and access instructions not provided in manuscript
Steerable sequence scale limited: Generates ~50 sequences per DMS assay; scale is modest compared to modern generative models and may limit practical protein design applications
Missing computational cost analysis: No discussion of GPU memory, training time, or computational overhead of CLT training despite O(L²) decoder complexity

strengths: Novel Cross-Layer Transcoder architecture that effectively captures inter-layer computation in protein language models, addressing a key limitation of SAE-based approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with three distinct tasks (circuit discovery, steering, biological motif recovery) and thorough ablation studies comparing multiple replacement model variants
Strong empirical results recovering 82-89% of model performance with only ~1.5% of latent space and successful steering of models toward high-fitness variants
Excellent reproducibility with released code, interactive visualization tool, complete hyperparameter specifications, and extensive implementation details in appendices
Successfully identifies known biological motifs (kinase domain, NADP+ binding sites, GB1 stability circuits) with detailed mechanistic analysis, demonstrating interpretability value
Addresses practical scalability concerns with windowed CLT approach reducing parameters by 40% while maintaining performance
weaknesses: Limited architectural generalization: evaluation predominantly on ESM2 with only brief scaling tests on ESM2-35M; claims about applicability to general protein language models not validated across other major architectures (ProtBERT, AlphaFold-based models, etc.)

Circuit interpretation validation relies heavily on manual biological analysis and post-hoc alignment with known motifs; limited systematic quantitative assessment of biological meaningfulness and only three detailed case studies
Scalability challenges not fully resolved: O(L²) decoder matrix scaling remains problematic for larger models, and windowed CLT solution is somewhat ad-hoc requiring model-specific tuning

Limited baseline comparisons: primarily compared against own baselines (PLT, direct models) with insufficient evaluation against other mechanistic interpretability methods, recent sparse autoencoders, or NLP circuit discovery approaches
Circular reasoning concern in validation: steering experiments use discovered circuits to prove their correctness, which is inherently self-validating; need for independent validation mechanisms
Statistical rigor issues: large error bars in some results, limited significance testing, small sample sizes in DMS experiments, and insufficient sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter choices

Limited biological validation: no wet lab demonstration of novel biological insights beyond steering; biological value remains largely theoretical with validation relying on steering and known motif alignment rather than experimental discovery

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baseline comparisons (PLT, CAA, random mutations) across three distinct tasks (circuit discovery, steering, biological motif identification)
Sound technical methodology for modeling inter-layer dependencies using cross-layer transcoder layers with clear mathematical formulation
Reproducibility provisions including committed code release, detailed hyperparameters, and provided visualization tools with interactive interface
Qualitative case studies (protein kinase domain, NADP+ binding, GB1) provide concrete examples of circuit localization capability
Thorough appendices with experimental details, multiple replacement model variants (direct, sequential, full), and ablation studies
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contributions are applications of existing techniques (sparse autoencoders, transcoders from prior work) without substantive algorithmic innovation

Unvalidated claims about biological discovery: claims to recover 'known biological motifs' based only on three qualitative case studies; biological plausibility is subjective visual inspection rather than systematic validation

Weak validation methodology: uses proxy tasks (next-token prediction) that may not align with protein function; CNN evaluation models trained by authors lack independent validation; DMS assay validation inconsistent in quality (some <100 unique sequences); Spearman correlations of 0.4-0.5 suggest circuits capture limited functional variance

Severely limited scope: evaluated exclusively on ESM2-8M; no results on other major pLM architectures (ProtBERT, OmegaFold); authors acknowledge extending to other architectures 'is not trivial'; dramatically limits generalizability

Unclear practical significance: understanding pLM circuits does not improve protein function prediction (82% performance recovery on classification); no demonstration that insights enable better protein design; interpretability without predictive benefit

Manual interpretation bottleneck: authors acknowledge circuits 'currently relies on manual analysis'; no automated validation of biological relevance; large circuits (79% of model) with minimal latent usage suggest potential over-parameterization
Incomplete comparison to alternatives: Appendix H shows sparse autoencoders (SAEs) perform similarly to CLTs; insufficient discussion of why CLTs are necessary if SAEs are equally effective
Scalability concerns: CLTs require O(L²) decoder matrices; windowed CLTs reduce parameters 40% but significantly hurt performance; unclear if approach scales to modern large pLMs

High variance in results: many results have error bars ±0.5+; Table 1 shows wide performance variance across DMS assays (mean scores 1.26±0.09 vs 0.32±0.14); steering experiments (Tables 6-7) show instability suggesting artifacts

strengths: Well-motivated technical framework using cross-layer transcoders that explicitly capture inter-layer computation, a principled advance over layer-wise approximations
Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct tasks (circuit discovery, steering, biological validation) with multiple DMS assays and strong baselines
Strong empirical results demonstrating 82% performance recovery on protein family classification while using <1% of latent space
Meaningful biological grounding with validation against known motifs (protein kinase domain, NADP+ binding, GB1 binding) and interpretable circuit features
Excellent reproducibility support including extensive implementation details, hyperparameter discussions, promised code release, and interactive visualization tool
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations rather than overselling results
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and good motivation connecting technical approach to biological interpretability
weaknesses: Limited architectural scope: focuses primarily on ESM2 (2023 model) with minimal evaluation on diverse recent pLM architectures; extension claims to diffusion models remain entirely speculative

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: CLTs scale with O(L²) parameters; proposed windowed CLTs reduce this but compromise modeling of distant layer dependencies with hyperparameter tuning appearing heuristic

Incomplete circuit interpretation methodology: heavy reliance on manual human annotation (only 3 detailed case studies provided), lacks quantitative interpretability metrics, minimal guidance for interpreting novel circuits without known biological matches

Biological validation limitations: circuits only validate known motifs rather than discovering novel mechanisms; steering experiments use self-referential CNN probe without independent experimental validation or empirical protein engineering results

Methodological concerns: circuit discovery uses greedy search without optimality guarantees, various thresholds and design choices appear arbitrary with limited sensitivity analysis, circular reasoning risk from shared training objectives

Insufficient baseline comparisons: SAEs receive dismissive treatment despite relevance (Appendix H only), missing recent mechanistic interpretability methods, PEX/GGS comparisons favor ProtoMech by design rather than fair comparison
Statistical rigor gaps: no formal significance testing despite many comparisons, marginal performance differences between methods, no multiple comparison correction across numerous DMS assays

Missing generalization analysis: no cross-task generalization (family classification→function prediction), unclear if circuits are ESM2-specific, insufficient evaluation of architectural generalizability
